messages.subject: model averaging in Stan
parts:
Hey everyone, 

I have a similar issue to what is described here:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/Bayesian$20model$20averaging$20without$20reversible-jump$20MCMC$20on$20highly-dimensional$20models%7Csort:relevance/stan-users/ixBFDRJj8Y0/Zag10wQlBQAJ

where I have several hierarchical regression models with different parameterizations and I'd like to combine them to make predictions. I'm first attempting to follow Andrew's weighted model approach described in that thread (before maybe looking into mixture modeling) and am unsure if my implementation is correct:

data{
  int<lower=0>  N;              //number of observations
  int<lower=0>  K;              //number of predictors
  matrix[N,K]     x;               //matrix of predictions
  vector[N]        y;               //response variable
}

parameters{
  simplex[K]    lambda;      //weights for each predictor
}

transformed parameters{
  real<lower=0> squared_error;
  squared_error = dot_self(y - x*lambda);
}

model{
  target += -squared_error;
}


Here I'm trying to find the ideal weights for each model by minimizing the sum of squared prediction errors. So from this I have a few questions:

1) am I on the right track with this implementation?
2) should I be using Stan's optimization methods here instead of sampling?


Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] model averaging in Stan
parts:
> On Dec 1, 2016, at 5:35 PM, Bryan Galvin <bcga...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hey everyone,
>
> I have a similar issue to what is described here:
>
> https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/Bayesian$20model$20averaging$20without$20reversible-jump$20MCMC$20on$20highly-dimensional$20models%7Csort:relevance/stan-users/ixBFDRJj8Y0/Zag10wQlBQAJ
>
> where I have several hierarchical regression models with different parameterizations and I'd like to combine them to make predictions.

We generally recommend model expansion rather than model averaging.
Just build one big model with all the predictors.

Or you can build a mixture model at the object level rather than
trying to fit and then mix. And we'd recommend regularization.

Historically, model averaging was just a stop-gap measure because
the full joint model would be too expensive to fit.

More below.

> I'm first attempting to follow Andrew's weighted model approach described in that thread (before maybe looking into mixture modeling) and am unsure if my implementation is correct:
>
> data{
> int<lower=0> N; //number of observations
> int<lower=0> K; //number of predictors
> matrix[N,K] x; //matrix of predictions
> vector[N] y; //response variable
> }
>
> parameters{
> simplex[K] lambda; //weights for each predictor
> }
>
> transformed parameters{
> real<lower=0> squared_error;
> squared_error = dot_self(y - x*lambda);
> }
>
> model{
> target += -squared_error;
> }
>
>
> Here I'm trying to find the ideal weights for each model by minimizing the sum of squared prediction errors. So from this I have a few questions:
>
> 1) am I on the right track with this implementation?

You could just write

y ~ normal(x * lambda, 1 / sqrt(2));

and avoid having to define the error yourself. It'll be a little
less inefficient (I'd suggest a scale of 1 rather than 1 / sqrt(2),
which you get from your version).
> 2) should I be using Stan's optimization methods here instead of sampling?

If you want the maximum likelihood fit, that's what you need to do.

- Bob
